mcqs.question: A candidate describes spending three days tracking down a hard-to-reproduce race condition as their "hardest technical decision." What's the issue with this story?
options: It's not hard enough — three days is too short to count as a difficult problem
It was a hard implementation problem with one correct fix, not a decision with real costs on both sides
Race conditions are never appropriate topics for this question
The story is fine as long as it's told with enough technical detail
mcqs.explanation: The question asks for a hard decision, meaning a choice where both options had a real cost. Finding a bug's root cause, however time-consuming, has one correct fix once found — it demonstrates persistence, not judgment under a genuine trade-off. Duration and technical detail don't change that distinction.

mcqs.question: In the two-options diagram, what indicates a decision was genuinely hard rather than obviously correct?
options: The chosen option has zero downsides listed
Both options have a real cost box, not just the one that was rejected
The decision was made quickly under time pressure
The rejected option was clearly worse on every axis
mcqs.explanation: A hard decision has a real cost attached to both options — if the chosen option has no downside, or the rejected one is worse on every axis, there was no genuine trade-off. Speed of the decision doesn't determine whether it was hard in this sense.

mcqs.question: The interviewer asks, "Would you make the same call again?" What is this follow-up actually testing?
options: Whether you'll defend your original decision unconditionally to appear consistent
Your ability to reason honestly with hindsight, whether that lands on yes or no
Whether you remember the exact reasoning you used at the time, word for word
Whether the original decision has since been proven wrong by the business
mcqs.explanation: This follow-up probes honest judgment, not loyalty to a past call or perfect recall. A well-reasoned yes and a well-reasoned, specific no are both strong answers; defensiveness reads worse than either. It isn't contingent on the business having since proven the decision wrong.
